4914.dq: A major distinction among the groups is that in TV and the Serran languages, the domain for stress is the word. In contrast, in the Cupan languages, prefixes are nearly always extrametrical (with exceptions to be noted for stressless roots), and the domain of stress is the root or stem.

4914.heavy: A short vowel counts as one mora and long vowel as two moras for the placement of stress. In Takic, syllable-final consonants also figure in the mora count, unlike the situation reported for Southern Paiute where the gemination or prenasalization of a consonant has no effect on stress placement (Sapir 1949:50-51).... A short vowel before another vowel does not count as a mora (and is often written as glide in the source materials)
4914.dflt: Second syllable (the syllable containing the second mora when the first syllable is light CV), e.g. hohuunar 'bears', honaar 'badger', a$aawt 'eagle'.
4914.prule: Primary stress falls on the syllable containing the second mora counted from the left edge of the phonological word, prefixes and reduplicative syllables included: a long vowel counts two moras and a coda consonant one, so an initial CVV or CVC syllable is stressed (huunar 'bear', paahonar 'great bear', aawverot), otherwise the second syllable (hohuunar 'bears', honaar 'badger', a$aawt 'eagle'); a short vowel before another vowel is non-moraic; enclitics are normally outside the count but may take stress after a short root.
4914.srule: Placement not given: the source says 'Little is known about secondary stress, so we describe only primary stress' (Takic-wide) and, for Tongva, 'There are very few examples in the Harrington notes with secondary stress indicated'; no secondary-stress rule is stated.

4918.heavy: Syllable weight (represented here on a scale from one to four) is assigned according to the following set of rules: A weight of one is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is a monophthong short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and which do not have a consonant coda. A weight of two is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is a monophthong short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and which have a consonant coda. A weight of three is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is either a monophthong medium-duration vowel (/a/, /i/, or /u/) or a diphthong consisting of a short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and a glide. A weight of four is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is either a monophthong long vowel (/e/, /o/, /ā/, or /æ/) or a diphthong consisting of a medium-duration or long vowel (i.e. any vowel other than /ə/ and /ɨ/) and a glide. (§2.5.2, p. 120, p. 143)
4918.dflt: When the last two visible syllables are of equal weight, stress falls on the penultimate visible syllable: /sɨp.sɨp/ 2.2 initial, /kar.kəu/ 3.3 initial, /cay.koy/ 4.4 initial, /ka.rɨ.ram/ 3.1.3 initial (= antepenult, medial weight-1 syllable skipped), /key.ga.təy/ 4.3.3 penult, /ay.mā.ro/ 4.4.4 penult. When only one visible syllable remains it is stressed regardless of position (/ə.dəlp/ 1.2 final, /a.gə/ 3.1 initial). No polysyllabic words of weight-1 syllables only are attested (fn. 39).
4918.prule: Single word stress in a right-edge two-syllable window over a four-degree weight scale (1 = open syllable with short /ə ɨ/; 2 = closed syllable with short /ə ɨ/; 3 = /a i u/ nucleus or short vowel + glide; 4 = long /e o ā æ/ or non-short vowel + glide). The rightmost weight-1 syllable is extrametrical; if only one visible syllable remains it is stressed; otherwise the heavier of the last two visible syllables is stressed, and if they are of equal weight the penultimate visible syllable is stressed (trochaic default). Correlates: greater loudness and higher pitch, not duration.
4918.srule: Not mentioned in Drinfeld 2024, Section 2.5 'Stress', pp. 117-132 (whole section, worked examples and Tables 2.30-2.32 read; full-text search of the dissertation for secondary/rhythmic/alternating stress finds nothing). The rules and all examples mark one stressed syllable per word.

4922.dq: In Tiriyó, there are two main prosodic phenomena: rhythmic stress (with the phonological word as its domain) and intonational contours (with the utterance as their domain). [p. 60]
4922.heavy: Heavy = non-(C)V syllables: (C)Vh, (C)VN, CViVj, CViVjh, CViVjN (types listed pp. 62-63, examples (30a-f)); h and N are the only codas. 'Non-(C)V syllables behave differently: they conserve their stress regardless of their position within the word... the presence of non-(C)V syllables disturbs the alternating stress pattern on following (C)V syllables: the pattern restarts with an unstressed syllable, as if a new word had begun.' [p. 62, scan]
4922.dflt: All-light words: every second syllable from the left, final never stressed (3: 010, 4: 0100, 5: 01010, 6: 010100, 7: 0101010, 8: 01010100, Table 2.7 p. 61); all-light bisyllables and monosyllables get no stress (00, 0), only a pitch drop in isolation.
4922.prule: Iterative iambic rhythmic stress over the phonological word, computed left to right: the final syllable is never stressed; every non-final heavy syllable (non-(C)V: (C)Vh, (C)VN, CViVj, CViVjh, CViVjN) is stressed and restarts the alternation after it; every second light syllable, counting from the word start or from the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. All-light words: 2nd, 4th, 6th... syllables stressed (apoto [a.pó:.to], kit-apoto-ma-ti [ki.tá:.po.tó:.ma.ti]). No culminative primary stress is identified (p. 71).
4922.srule: No primary/secondary hierarchy: every stress placed by rules (i)-(iii) (each non-final heavy syllable; every second light syllable counted from the word start or from the nearest heavy syllable; never the final syllable) is an equal rhythmic stress, and no single syllable is analysed as bearing primary stress -- 'aside from an impression that the last stressed syllable in a phonological word sounds stronger than the others, there seems to be no reason to analyze any single syllable in a phonological word as bearing primary stress' (Meira 1999: 71).

4924.tone: Dornan p. 61: 'There are at least three tones in the Sesarwa language, the high, middle and low', with minimal triples (hwee x3; |gaa x3). 4928.tone: Tswa is a tone language (H vs. toneless; Ugembe 2017, Kisseberth & Ugembe 2025). Neither modern source uses the word 'stress': Kisseberth & Ugembe 2025 p. 3 'The penult vowel in the intonational phrase is lengthened. There is a tonal contrast between whether a vowel has a High tone or not'; Gundane 2021 'a duração na penúltima sílaba é somente fonética nesta língua' and length is 'meramente demarcativo que geralmente ocorre na penúltima sílaba, na última ou ainda na primeira sílaba por razões enfáticas'. Gowlett 2003 (Zone S survey, §3.6) calls it a 'penultimate length-stress feature which signals the end of a phrase or sentence in declarative sentences... not used in interrogative and exclamatory sentences'. So the 1902 word-level penult 'accent' is the same non-contrastive penultimate prominence that modern work places at the intonational-phrase edge in a tone language.

tn.quote: The tone-bearing unit in Citshwa is the vowel. All vowels in Citshwa are basically short vowels … The penult vowel in the intonational phrase is lengthened. There is a tonal contrast between whether a vowel has a High tone or not. We indicate the presence of a H tone in the pronunciation with an acute mark over the vowel. … Adjacent H tones that are separated by downstep represent a sequence of independent H tones. We propose that the downstep that separates two independent H tones is a phonological rule that operates both inside words and also across words.

4930.dq: Bei meinen Aufzeichnungen habe ich keine Anzeichen für Druckakzent in phonemischer Funktion feststellen können und bezeichne ihn deshalb nicht. 4930.dloc: Rottland 1982, ch. 5 'Kalenjin', sec. 5.1.3.2 'Druckakzent', pp. 77-78 (Google Books excerpt chain; not verified against a page scan).
4930.prule: No word-stress rule. Tugen is an H/L tone language (Jerono 2011: two underlying tones H and L, downstep, super-H; tone distinguishes lexemes and marks case/definiteness). The only statement on stress is Rottland 1982's pan-Kalenjin one: no sign of stress in phonemic function in his recordings, so it is not marked; phonetically stressed syllables are audible and always coincide with a non-low (high or rising/falling) tone, i.e. audible prominence is a correlate of tone, not an independent positional rule.
4930.srule: Not mentioned in Rottland 1982, ch. 5 sec. 5.1.3 'Prosodische Erscheinungen' (5.1.3.2 Druckakzent and 5.1.3.3 Ton, pp. 77-79, read complete from the excerpt chain: stress denied phonemic function, audible prominence tied to non-low tone, no primary/secondary distinction), nor in Jerono 2011 (sec. 2.3 Tone, pp. 36-37; 'stress'/'accent' absent from the thesis) or Lodge 1995 (p. 31).

4932.prule: Prominence = lengthening of the penultimate vowel with a High tone on its first mora (falling contour), placed on the penult of the FINAL word of each Phonological Phrase (right edge of XP). 'First, long vowels occur in a very limited number of native Berber words.' §2.3.3.1 p. 89: 'Prior to investigating stress in Berber, it is important to attempt to create some generic principles that govern vowel length because of its importance to stress. These ‘affixes’ tend to make a stressed short vowel into a long stressed vowel.' Summary p. 98: 'The stressed vowel in verbs with zero suffixes, these are generally lengthened and stressed simultaneously.' So the 'heavy' syllable is a surface long vowel (mostly in Arabic loans, or after a geminate / CC cluster / emphatic, or word-final ū), not a phonemic CVV rhyme; coda consonants play no part. 4934.prule: Stress (non-phonemic, weak) falls on a long vowel wherever it stands in the word ('usually' p. 96, 'seem to always' p. 98); in words without a long vowel it falls on the first syllable. Morphology overrides the default: plural -âwin is always stressed, possessive -inwin, -nikmit, -is are stressed and shift the stress from the first syllable to the penult (áʕšuš ~ aʕšušínwin, ânu ~ anuníkmit); -an, negative proclitics and enclitics -asin, -ak are unstressed. Stated for Douiret; Appendix VI gives the same for Ouirsighen (Jerba) and Chninni (long vowels always/usually stressed regardless of position; polysyllables otherwise initial; plural and possessive affixes stressed).
4934.srule: No secondary-stress rule is stated. Fn. 39 (p. 95) defines a grave accent for 'secondary stress' in the notation, but §2.4.3 (pp. 95-98) and Appendix VI (pp. 384-389) give no placement for it.
